L16: # EGFR/HER2 Vaccine Study
L17: 
L18: A new cancer immunotherapy developed by research team at Yale University is being evaluated in this study led by 【3†Therajan LLC †therajan.com】
L19: 
L20: 【4†Image†static.wixstatic.com】
L21: # Why immunotherapy?
L22: 
L23:   * May prevent the recurrence and spreading of cancer
L24: 
L25:   * May help when surgery is not possible, or if chemotherapy stops working
L26: 
L27:   * May slow or reverse cancer metastasis
L28:

L58:   * Almost 12-month median survival time was reported for osteosarcoma patients who received palliative radiation plus vaccine WITHOUT amputation.
L59: 
L60:   * Longer median survival times (compared to chemotherapy alone) were reported for Stage 1 and Stage 2 hemangiosarcoma canine patients.
L61: 
L62: ​​
L63: They are early results with a small number of patients. More data is being collected.​​​
L64: 
L65: ​
L66: 
L67: An Introductory 【5†Quick Guide on Canine Cancer Immunotherapy can be downloaded here†ccralliance.myflodesk.com】.​
L68: 
L69: 【9†Image: Maggie 2023.jpg†static.wixstatic.com】
L70: 
L71: Maggie was diagnosed with osteosarcoma in Jan 2020 and got conventional treatment plus the vaccine.  She is still cancer-free.
L72: 
L73: 【10†Image: ranger_edited.jpg†static.wixstatic.com】
L74: Ranger's cancer kept on spreading, even after surgery and chemotherapy.  But his tumors shrank and disappeared after the EGFR/HER2 vaccine treatment.
L75: 
L76: 【11†Image: Codi_edited.jpg†static.wixstatic.com】
L77: 
L78: Codi's metastatic osteosarcoma began to disappear a month after he received the EGFR/HER2 vaccine injection. He enjoyed 3 extra years as a healthy, happy pup.
L79: 
L80: 【12†Learn More】
L81: # How does it work?
L82: 
L83:   * Safely activates the immune system against cancer cells that are over-expressing EGFR and HER2 proteins.
L84: 
L85:   * 【12†The vaccine has already been given to over 600 canine patients】. Minimum side effects reported.
L86: 
L87:   * May help with many different cancer types. Preliminary data for osteosarcoma and hemangiosarcoma published.
L88: 
L89:   * Watch a recent update from the team.
L90: # Limitations and Challenges
L91: 
L92:   * Today's immunotherapy cannot guarantee every dog will become a long-term survivor.
L93: 
L94:   * Researchers are investigating different ways to safely enhance the efficacy and increase the number of responders.
L95:

L68: # A New Drug for Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma in Dogs
L69: 
L70: Canine
L71: 
L72: 【26†Image: terrier looking at camera】
L73: 
L74: Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC) is the second most common oral malignant tumor in dogs. They are locally invasive and often recurrent. They invade the bone rapidly and sometimes cannot be removed by surgery.
L75: Trametinib is an oral medication approved by the FDA for use in certain types of cancer in humans and has been previously found to be safe in dogs under experimental conditions. We have found that some dogs with oral squamous cell carcinomas respond very favorably to the drug, while others do not. This is an expanded study to learn more about why some of these cancers respond well so we can target therapy most effectively.
L76: Eligibility: Dogs seen by the Cornell University Hospital for Animals (CUHA) who have been diagnosed with an oral squamous cell carcinoma are eligible.
L77: 
L78: Compensation: All visits and procedures directly related to and during the study will be performed entirely free of charge to you. The drug will also be provided to you free of charge. Additionally, if your dog completes the study, the study will cover an additional $1000 worth of medical expenses related to standard of care therapy for your dog's SCC.
L79: Owner Responsibilities: We will ask you to bring your dog to the CUHA for follow up appointments on or around days 14, 42, 70, 108, and 126 after enrollment. On days 14, 42, 70 and 108 we will conduct a physical and oral examination under light sedation.
L80: On day 126, we will do a physical exam and perform a full-body CT scan under general anesthesia to document response to treatment, obtain a tumor tissue sample and perform a fine-needle aspirate of the mandibular (under the jaw) lymph nodes for microscopic and genetic analyses.
L81: You are also committing to sharing clinical information by means of a short questionnaire to be completed at each visit, or by attending a short weekly phone call to allow us to closely monitor and document any side effects.
L82: Finally, you are committing to give the medicine by mouth once daily. This medication is considered chemotherapy and safety instructions will be relayed to you. We will also ask you to complete a brief questionnaire about your dog's health once a week (either over the phone or in person at the visits).
L83: 
L84: Principal Investigator: Santiago Peralta, DVM, AVDC, FF-AVDC-OMFS
L85: Contact/Schedule an Appointment: If you have a dog you think may be eligible please call either the dentistry service or the oncology service or the clinical trials coordinator at 607.253.3060, or email vet-research@cornell.edu
L86: 
L87: Sponsor: This clinical trial is sponsored by the 【27†Cornell Richard P. Riney Canine Health Center】

L68: # Smart-Start Therapy for Canine B-Cell Lymphoma
L69: 
L70: Canine
L71: 
L72: 【26†Image: older golden retriever getting petted on head】
L73: 
L74: Lymphoma is one of the most common cancers we see in dogs. The current standard treatment — a combination chemotherapy protocol called CHOP — has been used for decades and can put most dogs into remission. Unfortunately, the cancer usually comes back within 6 to 12 months, and once it returns, it becomes much harder to treat.
L75: We also know that CHOP has real drawbacks for families and their dogs: It's a big commitment. Treatment represents a significant financial investment and requires frequent visits to the veterinary hospital over several months.
L76: 
L77: Side effects can happen. Most dogs tolerate chemotherapy well, but some experience side effects that affect their quality of life.
L78: 
L79: Results haven't improved much over time. Despite years of use, survival times with CHOP have stayed roughly the same.
L80: Perhaps most importantly, every dog currently receives the same chemotherapy — even though we know lymphoma doesn't behave the same way in every patient.
L81: This study takes a more personalized path. By looking closely at the unique biology of each dog's cancer — including the environment surrounding the tumor cells — we can better understand why some dogs respond well to treatment and others don't. We then use that information to guide a "Smart-Start" treatment strategy, matching each dog with the therapy most likely to help them from the very beginning.
L82: 
L83: Our goals are twofold:
L84:   1. Get better results from the treatments we already have by choosing the right approach for each individual dog.
L85:   2. Build the foundation for the next generation of lymphoma care — treatments that target the specific biology of the cancer and, over time, rely less on traditional chemotherapy.
L86: 
L87: We hope this is a step toward smarter, more individualized cancer care for dogs — with the hope of longer, healthier remissions and a gentler treatment experience along the way.
L88: Eligibility: Dogs seen by the Cornell University Hospital for Animals (CUHA) who have been diagnosed with B-cell lymphoma, have had no prior treatment other than prednisolone, and are willing to pursue standard of care chemotherapy are eligible.
L89: Compensation: There are no extra costs to you if your dog participates in the study. You will be charged our usual fees for any tests or procedures for your dog’s care except for those that are done specifically for the study. There will be a 10% discount on anything that isn’t covered on study related visits. The 10% hospital discount will be given on all standard of care chemotherapy visits.
L90: Further, as an incentive for enrollment, the study will provide $1000 towards the cost of chemotherapy for your dog.
L91: Owner Responsibilities: Your commitments and responsibilities are: bringing your dog to Cornell oncology service for appointments, during which samples (blood, fine needle aspirate) will be taken for diagnostic purposes and an extra volume will be taken for the study. Dogs will be assigned the pre-treatment drug based on the type of tumor. There is no placebo in this study.
L92: The pre-treatment drug is either an oral tablet given four times over a 14-day window or an injection given on five consecutive days at the CUHA.
L93: You will then be asked to come back for routine CHOP chemotherapy visits and we will ask to collect one more set of blood samples when your dog completes CHOP.
